title: The Mole, the Hedgehog, and the Quiz Night
markdown:
The moon, a sliver of polished pearl, climbed over the sleepy village. Quiz night at the Greenhouse Garden Café usually meant whispering ferns and bees. Tonight a different hum built: nervous, anticipatory. For Jonah the mole, caretaker of the most magnificent greenhouse this side of the Whispering Woods, it sent mild burrowing dread straight to his whiskers.

He had spent the afternoon watering, staking, and whispering to orchids that did not need a pep talk and received one anyway. Prize petunias shimmered like crushed jewels. Tomatoes blushed like rosy cheeks. He checked the slightly ajar door twice and still did not quite latch it. A quiz, he told himself, was only questions. The greenhouse was the real examination, and he sat it every dawn.

He loved the place with a devotion usually reserved for ancient trees or first dawn. Prize petunias shimmered like crushed jewels; tomatoes blushed like rosy cheeks. The air was damp earth, sweet nectar, the spicy tang of marigolds. He knew every leaf, every tendril, every corner where a shy dewdrop hid. Quiz nights were different soil. People. Lots of people, rustling like startled sparrows. Competition. The air felt thick with it, not only jasmine but a prickling unease that clung like dew.

“Just a few more minutes, my dears,” he murmured to orchids whose velvety petals unfurled like miniature alien landscapes. He polished his spectacles case, smooth wood a comfort. “A united, dignified front.” He imagined himself a towering oak. He felt like a dandelion puff.

The café bell chimed, a tiny tinkling alarm. In stepped Iorwen Bristleback, a hedgehog whose spines gleamed with ethereal politeness, tiny polished needles. Iorwen was unnervingly agreeable. Everything they said came wrapped in such gentle consideration that irritation and grudging admiration arrived together: rose petals, pretty and sticky.

“Good evening, Jonah. Might I say, your greenhouse is looking particularly resplendent. The evening air is quite exquisite. A gentle caress, wouldn’t you agree?”

Jonah managed a tight whiskery smile. “Iorwen. Yes. It’s… air.” He had hoped for a shared sigh about the absurdity. Iorwen offered another serene nod, nose twitching with mild genuine interest.

Reginald Flutterwing, a perpetually cheerful robin, flapped onto a wobbly perch of old seed catalogues. “Welcome, one and all. Tonight we delve into general knowledge. Questions to tickle brains and perhaps funny bones. We begin with The Grand Gallery of Gallant Goats.”

Each question felt like a hidden root waiting to trip Jonah. He had secured a table near the back, hoping to blend into fig-tree shadows, broad leaves like silent hands. Iorwen settled opposite, bright intelligent eyes scanning with a calm that made Jonah’s paws twitch. Two stones in a stream; he felt a bobbing twig.

Round one: Famous Bridges. “The Tower Bridge, London,” Reginald chirped. Murmur, frantic scribbling. Jonah’s velvety paw left an ink smudge. Iorwen wrote without a quill-stroke out of place, posture as straight as a budding daffodil.

Round two: Types of Cheese. “Gorgonzola Dolce.” Jonah was fairly sure, having once nibbled a pungent piece a forgetful visitor left. A rogue draft from the slightly ajar door he had forgotten to secure sent crimson, gold, and snow-white petals dancing in a miniature blizzard. Hot flush; ears flat. Iorwen merely tilted their head as if observing an interesting dust mote.

Then the vexing ones. “Average speed of a migrating goose?” Iorwen, with a serene sigh, wrote thirty miles per hour, give or take a prevailing wind. Jonah’s jaw dropped. He had spent weeks watching geese—honks, formations, trajectory across the sky—and never once considered their average speed. What did goose velocity have to do with dahlias reaching full glorious potential?

The greenhouse keeps us both, he thought, absurdly, watching Iorwen’s calm, and clung to the phrase as if it were a pot that would not tip.

Rounds continued, each a tiny polite ordeal. Iorwen answered with effortless grace and a soft “If I may be so bold” that was both humble and devastatingly accurate. Jonah fought a silent desperate battle with dignity. A ladybug, red jewel with black dots, landed on his nose; he sneezed a puff of earth onto his spectacles. Pipkin Squeakerton, a flustered dormouse waiter, tripped on ivy and sent a teacup skittering toward Jonah’s Venus flytraps, toothy mouths snapping. Each pinprick threatened his stoic balloon. He imagined composure as a glass dome and the quiz as a persistent woodpecker.

Reginald announced the penultimate: Peculiar Plant Potions. A gasp. Specialised knowledge, dedicated gardeners. Jonah’s soil. His domain. A flicker of hope.

Iorwen tilted their head. “Peculiar potions. One does wonder about the precise efficacy of a dewdrop infused with moonbeam. A delicate balance.”

Then the outrageous thing. A stronger gust roared through the open door. Not only petals: leaves, dirt, and a rather large very ripe tomato that detached and hurtled like a small red cannonball. It smacked Reginald’s seed catalogues, sending robin, perch, and questions cascading.

Chaos. Pipkin dropped a tray of acorn scones; they bounced under tables like runaway marbles. The air, usually rosemary and lemon balm, carried the sharp smell of rising steam from collective concentration and mild panic.

Jonah, normally reserved, lunged—not to answer, to steady a toppling display of prize cacti. Then, with surprising speed, he scooped scattered scones. “Careful. Don’t want anyone pricked by a rogue prickle.”

He did not speak after that. He worked: righting a pot, gathering a scone, setting a catalogue page back on Reginald’s stack, earth on his paws, tomato pulp on the floor. A cactus leaned; he caught it. Another scone rolled toward the ivy; he scooped it. Silent toil while the greenhouse held its breath around him. No clever answer. No polite sigh. Only paws that knew soil better than scores. The greenhouse keeps us both.

Pipkin froze mid-apology. A competitor under a neighbouring table blinked at the rescued cacti as if they had become the real quiz. Jonah kept moving until the last scone sat, slightly dusty, on a tray, and the catalogues made a crooked but standing pile.

Iorwen observed with wide innocent eyes, brow only slightly furrowed, as if solving a riddle in a nature journal, and offered a small polite sigh of contentment.

Too much. The pressure, the incessant politeness, the competence even in pandemonium. Jonah’s facade crumbled not with a crash but with a quiet apologetic sigh, a wilting petal letting go. He leaned forward, dignity forgotten.

“Iorwen. This is rather a lot.”

No judgment. A gentle inquiry, open as a dew-kissed flower. “Is it? I find focused thought invigorating. A complex puzzle. Though the geese were an unexpected variable. And that tomato. A projectile of remarkable velocity.”

Honesty arrived like first sun after a long night. “It is not the geese. Or the tomato. It is that you are so good at it. And so impossibly polite. And I am trying not to uproot a prize begonia with a sneeze. Or sneeze dirt into your answers. Or get impaled by a scone.”

Iorwen smiled, genuine, eyes crinkling like morning dew. Formality thinned to warmth. “Jonah. The snails are fascinating, all those tiny trails. But the true marvel is how you keep these delicate blooms thriving through every season. The vibrancy you coax from soil is a knowledge far greater than goose-speed or tomato-dodging. A deep magic that feeds the world. And frankly, your scone-scooping is nothing short of heroic.”

Relief, warm as a freshly baked scone. Not a competition. Knowledge. That admiration, simply sincere, was worth more than any prize.

Reginald, dusted with catalogue pages and tomato pulp, regained his perch. “After that eventful interlude, the results. The winners are Iorwen Bristleback and their team.” A small gracious bow; spines rustled.

As others packed, a quiet understanding passed. Jonah’s fear of looking clumsy had made the evening a trial. Iorwen had seen past the quiz to the living garden.

“Perhaps next time we could identify composting materials,” Jonah ventured, a shy flower of a smile. “Decomposition rates. Nitrogen and carbon. Fascinating. And I promise, no rogue tomatoes.”

Iorwen’s eyes lit. “Delightful. A topic where my knowledge is somewhat less developed. Observable phenomena are more my realm. Enlighten me? And don’t worry about the scones. I have always suspected excellent aerodynamic properties.”

They walked out together. The moon was a proud disc, long silver shadows. Steam gone; cool evening, night-blooming jasmine. Jonah had faced the dread not by winning but by being honest, and found a friend. The greenhouse keeps us both. He locked the door on orchids that had not needed to be dignified after all, only watered, and on a hedgehog whose politeness had been, under the spines, simply kindness.
characters: Jonah (mole greenhouse caretaker), Iorwen Bristleback (hedgehog quiz rival)
